item.title: Why this is no disaster for Polanski: Greens remain competitive as voters reward Burnham
item.description:
Why this is no disaster for Polanski: Greens remain competitive as voters reward Burnham

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Fri, 10/09/2026 - 10:21
The Green vote share surged to a historic high in Holborn and St Pancras, despite the party leader losing to Labour
Green Party leader Zack Polanski reacts following the results in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, triggered by the resignation of Keir Starmer as MP, 9 October (Reuters/Toby Shepheard)
Off

Is this the end of Zack Polanski as leader of the Green Party? Many seem to think so - indeed, multiple national newspapers have suggested it.

No doubt there are people in his party who want him out now he’s failed to be elected to parliament for Holborn and St Pancras.

But on closer examination, Polanski’s defeat on Friday morning is far less of a catastrophe than many of his critics are claiming.

The Green vote share surged to a historic high in the seat, and with a volatile electorate there are clear signs that the party can be optimistic about its potential for future growth.

This is undeniably a victory for Andy Burnham. Labour’s candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali - with one of the most unusual backstories in British politics, as a child refugee from Somalia who enjoyed enormous success in local politics and rose to become leader of Camden Council - is locally well-known and popular.

Ironically, Abdi-Wali is an ally of Keir Starmer, who she will replace in parliament, and her political positions have often seemed closer to Starmer’s than the new prime minister’s.

Yet there’s little doubt that her win is in no small part a reflection of the "Burnham bounce" in the national polls. 

'We're waiting to sweep up their votes': Three days inside the Green Party conference
Read More »

In the ethnically diverse Holborn and St Pancras, where the Gaza genocide remains a salient issue, many voters will have almost certainly wanted to reward the Burnham government for its recent sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements.

Many voters, meanwhile, will simply be relieved that Starmer is gone and replaced by a more personable figure. 

Burnham is showing Labour can defend its seats and is clawing back votes it lost under Starmer. 

But this by-election won’t particularly embolden Labour strategists who are mulling an early general election next spring.

The Green Party gave Labour a serious run for its money, with Polanski winning 8,928 votes (32.8 percent) to Abdi-Wali’s 12,292 (45.2 percent).

Labour’s majority, just 3,364 votes, is extremely slim. By comparison Starmer’s majority was 11,572 votes in the 2024 general election, and even then his had been significantly slashed by independent candidate Andrew Feinstein. 

Remember that Holborn and St Pancras is historically a Labour stronghold. That status quo hasn’t exactly returned. 

Polanski has changed the party's fortunes

Many in the Green Party see Polanski’s decision to stand for election during Burnham’s honeymoon phase as a significant miscalculation. 

In the short term this by-election will likely deal a heavy blow to the party’s momentum and image. 

But look at what the Greens have achieved in the past year.

The party surged in the polls late last year after Polanski was elected leader. The Greens gained further momentum and credibility with a by-election victory in Gorton and Denton in February and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did.

'It’s a setback, not doom. We are the biggest threat to the establishment'

- Asma Alam, Green councillor

Polanski is at least partially responsible for Starmer's downfall and Burnham's premiership. This means the Greens are now suffering from their own success.

The party’s polling nationally has plummeted and is close to where it was in 2024. Crucially, however, in target seats - like London's Holborn and St Pancras - it is still performing strongly. 

It was never likely that Polanski could replicate the historic victory in Gorton and Denton, which mobilised both huge anti-Starmer sentiment and opposition to the visceral local threat of Reform. 

Yet Friday's was still the Green Party’s second best by-election result ever. Polanski has indisputedly changed the party’s fortunes. 

Hostile media

“The result is really sad, but we always knew this was going to be a tight battle,” Asma Alam, a Green councillor and campaign coordinator, told Middle East Eye on Friday morning.

“All this noise about new leadership needed is rubbish,” she added. “Zack won the leadership by a significant majority - that won’t change. 

“It’s a setback, not doom. We are the biggest threat to the establishment.”

Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali told MEE at the party’s conference last weekend that "what we can continue to do is make sure that we’re holding the government to account".

Ali added that if the Greens "are continuously providing better alternatives, the Labour government is going to have to take notice.

"And if they don't, then we're waiting to sweep up their votes."

The Greens have much to reflect on, including how the party can effectively deal with hostile media coverage, which will only increase. 

The by-election came after days of vociferous attacks on the Greens in the national media over the party conference vote last weekend to declare Zionism a form of racism. 

There is no evidence that anger over the conference vote played a role in influencing the by-election, but it is nonetheless likely that the barrage of hostile media coverage of Polanski and the Greens will have put off some undecided voters.

Everything to play for

Significantly, the "Zionism is racism" motion, which dominated media coverage of the conference, involved Green activists, not the leadership, shaping the agenda.

Polanski wasn’t even at the conference for the vote itself - he expressed discomfort with elements of the motion, although he said he thinks Zionism is racist - because he was campaigning in Holborn. 

Green Party recognises Zionism as a form of racism and backs single Palestinian state
Read More »

“I refute the idea that the motion impacted the results,” Alam said. “What it lost in potential votes it also added in votes from people who preferred our strong stance.”

But Caroline Lucas, a former Green leader, has heaped criticism on Polanski, suggesting he failed to show leadership on the issue of the Zionism motion, which she strongly opposed.

Will the Greens now seek to change the party’s internal system to give the leadership more control over the formulation of policy? This may be necessary for the party’s growth, but it would trigger a revolt among the membership. 

Internally, the Greens have tough questions which they need to resolve.

Ultimately, though, the key lesson from Polanski’s performance in Holborn and St Pancras is that the electorate is still volatile.

Since the 2024 election we have seen the implosion of the two-party political system. With Burnham in power, many pundits have prophesied its return. 

This has not happened yet, as the close competition in the by-election indicates. Depending on the Burnham government’s performance, support for the Greens could either plummet further or surge again. Voters are less loyal than they once were and no party can take them for granted.

For both Labour and the Greens, then, there's everything to play for.

item.title: Israel kills eight in Gaza as families forced to flee homes
item.description:
Israel kills eight in Gaza as families forced to flee homes

Israeli forces killed eight Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Thursday as they issued fresh expulsion orders in several areas, according to local reports.

A woman and a child were killed in strikes on two houses in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City, minutes after residents were told to leave.

One resident said he received a call from an Israeli officer ordering people to evacuate.

Panic ensued as families rushed to flee, but not everyone managed to escape before the bombing, according to the Anadolu news agency.

Elsewhere in Gaza City, Israeli forces ordered residents in the Old City, in the east, to evacuate ahead of further strikes.

In southern Gaza, Israeli forces also issued evacuation orders for two areas after bombing them.

An Israeli soldier shot and killed a Palestinian in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza. Two more people were killed when a car was bombed near the Jordanian Field Hospital in Gaza City.

The latest strikes and forced displacement come a day before the first anniversary of a ceasefire announced to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, launched in October 2023 after the Hamas-led attack in southern Israel.

item.title: Iran determined to expand ties with Russia, Pezeshkian says
item.description:
Iran determined to expand ties with Russia, Pezeshkian says

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said relations between Tehran and Moscow are expanding, with trade, economic ties and communication progressing positively, according to the Iranian state news agency IRNA.

Speaking after meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Turkmenistan, Pezeshkian said Iran is determined to deepen its ties with Russia in line with the two sides’ joint strategic roadmap.

Pezeshkian also said that now is an appropriate opportunity for both countries to consolidate and expand their partnership.

item.title: Navi Pillay, eminent South African jurist, awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
Navi Pillay, eminent South African jurist, awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Fri, 10/09/2026 - 10:28
Pillay was the chair of the UN committee that concluded last year that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza, and is currently an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice
Former United Nations rights chief Navi Pillay pictured in Johannesburg in 2023 (Wikus de Wet/AFP)
Off

Navi Pillay, the eminent South African jurist who co-authored the United Nations report accusing Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced on Friday.

The committee said Pillay had been chosen "for her efforts to promote peace and international law".

"The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted," the committee said.

Pillay, 85, is one of the most influential figures in international criminal justice and human rights law, and is South Africa’s most prominent international judge. 

In her first reaction to the announcement, Pillay noted her last work as the the chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded in an authoritative report last year that Israel is responsible for genocide in Gaza. 

"The last thing I did is the report on Gaza naming what is happening there as genocide," she told a gathering of friends and colleagues at courtroom 600 at the Nuremberg Palace of Justice in Germany. "One of the main reactions to that report [was] paying tribute to me for my courage.. why would you need courage to speak the truth?" she said at the historic venue which hosted the post-World War II war crimes trials of the Nazis. 

A former UN high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014, Pillay was nominated by Nelson Mandela, then the president of South Africa, in 1995 to serve on the UN's International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), where she served as a judge and president (1999-2003). Pillay's work at the ICTR produced the first genocide convictions in history. 

She was also one of the founding judges of the International Criminal Court, and currently serves as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is due to determine whether the Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.

As the president of the ICTR, Pillay helped establish that rape and sexual violence can constitute genocide, setting a historic precedent in the jurisprudence on genocide.

In a wide-ranging interview with Middle East Eye's Expert Witness podcast last year, Pillay said that as a UN expert investigating genocide in Gaza she found "a lot of similarities" with her previous work on sexual violence as a form of genocide. 

Exclusive: Navi Pillay on Israel's Gaza genocide and global complicity
Read More »

"The commission finds a lot of similarities in the Akayesu case and what is currently unfolding in Gaza," she told MEE, referring to the landmark ICTR case that delivered the first conviction where rape was recognised as an act of genocide.

"We found that the widespread and gender-based violence was instrumentalised, not only as punishment against the individuals, but as part of a pattern of collective punishment to fracture, humiliate, and subjugate the Palestinian population in its entirety," she said.

"I was recognised for having delivered that first judgment and for writing that portion of it. That jurisprudence is directly applicable to the Gaza situation."

The Nobel prize committee recognised Pillay's work at the UN commission, as well as her contribution to setting precedents at international court cases.

"History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges - those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos - are therefore highly deserving of our praise," said the committee.

"But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination - qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench."

item.title: UN Security Council extends Sudan sanctions until 11th December
item.description: The United Nations Security Council on Thursday unanimously adopted a US-drafted resolution extending the sanctions regime imposed on Sudan for two months, until 11th December 2026. All 15 council members voted in favour of the resolution, which extends sanctions established under Security Council Resolution 1591, including an arms embargo. The resolution also extended the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the Sudan Sanctions Committee until 11th January 2027. The decision comes amid disagreements between the Sudanese military leadership and the US administration over responsibility for the country’s situation and the military’s rejection of what it describes as external interference.
